Replying to @naomi when pricing my pieces I consider time spent making/decorating/signing/waxing/glazing/sanding/lustering/firing/invetorying. I have done time studies to help gauge the time I spend on making the pieces. I also consider materials used. I apply gold luster to almost every piece and it’s expensive and requires an additional firing which is also another expense. I also consider experience. I have been working with clay for 14 years now so I consider all of those years of working to this point in my pieces value as well. Pricing is hard! Placing a value on your art is uncomfortable. I’m just happy to be here and I’m doing my best with the knowledge I have gained so far on this journey. I don’t think there is a right answer that will work for everyone, I’m just trying to do what feels right to me! pricing my work is truly my LEAST favourite thing 😭  especially after trying to look closer at the numbers behind my small ceramic business. i’m trying to map out the potential 1, 3, and 5 year revenue and expense projections to see if investing in a kiln and building this business actually makes any sense. at my current $30-$65 price point, i’m losing money selling my work and cannot justify a kiln. i’ve made the terrifying decision to raise my prices by 25-30%. the money will go towards expanding production (investing. in a kiln & shelving), upgrading my website, expanding to ship to the US, and finally, offering private lessons and workshops.  with the price increase, I will still need to survive 6 months - 1 year without a livable wage / making profit. i’ll be focusing on my higher-margin petal bowls and bring in some more affordable $25 products like spoon rests and trinket dishes to keep things as accessible as possible. my mugs are not viable as they take me 2hrs each, but i’m going to keep making them for now and hope i can speed it up. no more lidded jars outside of speciality collections as the margins are too low.  i’m also going to try to secure 1-2 freelance social media clients to provide me with some supplement income as a buffer. this is the behind the scenes of small ceramics business’ that you normally don’t see, because it’s not nearly as cute or fun as the pots themselves. #potterybusiness #ceramics #smallbusiness #priceincrease #handmadeceramics

When pulling larger amounts of clay we need to stop and think of the limitations of our material alongside the additional weight. Pulling a cylinder on 1-3lbs of clay is different from pulling a cylinder on 5+lbs of clay. This is due to the immense amount of weight that is being supported by base of our vessel. If we thin out this base too early on we risk failure due to collapse. These thin walls at the bottom of the vessel struggle to support the weight above it in conjunction with the force caused by the centrifugal force of the wheel when moving it. To resolve this issue we must begin or first pull higher up the vessel. I choose to begin at the middle with my first pull to even out this weight and force. Then move my way back down to the bottom. #harleyweiglestudio #potterytutorials

In my YouTube video this weekend I’m recreating some pots I haven’t thrown since 2014, specially store jars with inset, internal galleries and thin lids with thrown knobs. You can find a link to the fully narrated video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   I’ve lied a little bit. I did create jars that were similar to this during my apprenticeship with Lisa Hammond between 2014-2017, yet they were bellied pieces with a gallery closer to the jars I make these days, yet they unusual thrown knobs that were in themselves similar to small bowls.   To create pots with internal galleries like this you need to split the rim. One section becomes the lip, the other is coaxed inside and carefully set horizontal to essentially become a ledge onto which the lid can be held aloft. This alone is a tricky task and it involves throwing a form with enough material in the lip to withstand such a manoeuvre. Secondly, there’s the small disc-like lid, a form that’s thrown off-the-hump and then the following day it’s trimmed back to have its more exacting shape and the knob is thrown on, again, a tricky task as it involves fiddly, fingertip throwing and a lot of accuracy.   All of this and more will be covered in my longer, narrated YouTube upload. I enjoyed making these and since it has been such a long time since I’ve crafted them, my skillset in the interim has improved massively, thus I could apply newly learnt techniques and ability into making shapes I used to struggle with to some degree. I hope you like the film if you happen to click over and watch it, it’s greatly appreciated if you do as it helps to keep the lights on in the workshop.   #pottery #ceramics #handmade #jar #satisfying

Here’s an easy way to create a bold and dynamic surface design without spending hours nitpicking. This technique starts with a simple cylinder and a handful of slip, but the real magic comes from how the slip is applied while the wheel is spinning. One of the biggest game changers is sieving your slip multiple times before applying it. That silky smooth consistency helps the slip move naturally across the form instead of having clay chunks or inconsistencies. I also like pre-trimming a small foot before adding texture. It catches the excess slip and makes cleanup much easier later by not disturbing the texture during the trimming phase. As the glaze melts over these ridges, it naturally breaks across the high points and exposes flashes of the iron-rich clay underneath. That variation is what gives every single piece its own personality. It’s fast, expressive, and one of my favorite ways to create texture that feels organic and alive.
